s.en: Control the systemd system and service manager
s.es: controla systemd: servicios, unidades, arranque y apagado

start.es: Inicia la unidad ahora. No la activa en el arranque.
start.en: Start the unit now. Does not enable it at boot.

restart.es: Detiene e inicia la unidad (corta el servicio un instante).
restart.en: Stop and start the unit (briefly interrupts the service).

reload.es: Recarga la configuración sin parar el servicio (si lo admite).
reload.en: Reload configuration without stopping the service (if supported).

reload-or-restart.es: Recarga si puede; si no, reinicia.

enable.es: Hace que la unidad arranque automáticamente al iniciar el sistema (con --now, también la inicia).
enable.en: Make the unit start automatically at boot (with --now, also start it).

disable.es: Quita el arranque automático (no la detiene si está en marcha).
disable.en: Remove automatic start at boot (does not stop it if running).

status.es: Muestra el estado, el PID y las últimas líneas del registro.
status.en: Show the state, PID and last log lines.

is-active.es: Indica si la unidad está activa (código 0 = sí).
is-active.en: Tell whether the unit is active (exit 0 = yes).

is-enabled.es: Indica si arranca en el inicio.
is-enabled.en: Tell whether the unit starts at boot.

is-failed.en: Tell whether the unit has failed.

mask.es: Bloquea la unidad: no se puede iniciar ni siquiera a mano.
mask.en: Block the unit: it cannot be started, even manually.

daemon-reload.es: Relee los archivos de unidad (tras editarlos).

list-unit-files.es: Lista los archivos de unidad y si están habilitados.
list-unit-files.en: List unit files and whether they are enabled.

edit.es: Edita un archivo de unidad (crea un override).
edit.en: Edit a unit file (creates an override).

show.es: Muestra todas las propiedades de la unidad.
show.en: Show all properties of the unit.

isolate.es: Cambia a un objetivo (target), parando lo que no pertenezca a él.
isolate.en: Switch to a target, stopping everything not part of it.

set-default.es: Fija el objetivo de arranque por defecto.

get-default.es: Muestra el objetivo de arranque por defecto.

kill.es: Envía una señal a los procesos de la unidad.
kill.en: Send a signal to the unit's processes.

o.es: Con enable/disable/mask, además inicia o detiene la unidad ahora.
o.en: With enable/disable/mask, also start or stop the unit now.

o.es: No usa paginador (útil en guiones y capturas).
o.en: Do not pipe output into a pager.

o.es: Actúa sobre las unidades del usuario, no del sistema.
o.en: Talk to the service manager of the calling user.

o.es: Filtra por tipo de unidad (service, socket, timer…).
o.en: The argument should be a comma-separated list of unit types.
List units in failed state.
Show all units, including inactive ones.
Do not ellipsize unit names, process tree entries.
Suppress printing of the results of various commands.
When used with enable, overwrite any existing conflicting symlinks.

The argument is a comma-separated list of unit LOAD, SUB, or ACTIVE states. When listing units with list-units, list-dependencies, show or status, show only those in the specified states. Use --state=failed or --failed to show only failed units.

Equivalent to --value --property=, i.e. shows the value of the property without the property name or "=". Note that using -P once will also affect all properties listed with -p/--property=. Added in version 246.
When listing units, also show units of local containers. Units of local containers will be prefixed with the container name, separated by a single colon character (":"). Added in version 212.

Show reverse dependencies between units with list-dependencies, i.e. follow dependencies of type WantedBy=, RequiredBy=, UpheldBy=, PartOf=, BoundBy=, instead of Wants= and similar. Added in version 203.

With list-dependencies, show the units that are ordered before the specified unit. In other words, recursively list units following the After= dependency. Note that any After= dependency is automatically mirrored to create a Before= dependency.

With list-dependencies, show the units that are ordered after the specified unit. In other words, recursively list units following the Before= dependency. When passed to the list-jobs command, for each printed job show which other jobs it is waiting for.

When used with status, cat, list-units, and list-unit-files, those commands print all specified units and the dependencies of those units. Options --reverse, --after, --before may be used to change what types of dependencies are shown. Added in version 245.
When printing properties with show, only print the value, and skip the property name and "=". Also see option -P above. Added in version 230.
When showing sockets, show the type of the socket. Added in version 202.

When queuing a new job, this option controls how to deal with already queued jobs. It takes one of "fail", "lenient", "replace", "replace-irreversibly", "isolate", "ignore-dependencies", "ignore-requirements", "flush", "triggering", or "restart-dependencies".

When enqueuing a unit job (for example as effect of a systemctl start invocation or similar), show brief information about all jobs enqueued, covering both the requested job and any added because of unit dependencies. Note that the output will only include jobs immediately part of the transaction requested.
Shorthand for --job-mode=fail. When used with the kill command, if no units were killed, the operation results in an error. Added in version 227.

When system shutdown or sleep state is requested, this option controls checking of inhibitor locks. It takes one of "auto", "yes", and "no". Defaults to "auto", which means logind will perform the check and respect active inhibitor locks, but systemctl will only do a client-side check for interactive invocations (i.e.
Shortcut for --check-inhibitors=no. Added in version 198.

Just print what would be done. Currently supported by verbs halt, poweroff, reboot, kexec, suspend, hibernate, hybrid-sleep, suspend-then-hibernate, default, rescue, emergency, and exit. Added in version 236.
Display unit log output while executing unit operations. Added in version 258.

Do not generate the warnings shown by default in the following cases: • when systemctl is invoked without procfs mounted on /proc/, • when using enable or disable on units without install information (i.e.

Do not synchronously wait for the requested operation to finish. If this is not specified, the job will be verified, enqueued and systemctl will wait until the unit's start-up is completed. By passing this argument, it is only verified and enqueued. This option may not be combined with --wait.

When used with start or restart, synchronously wait for started units to terminate again. This option may not be combined with --no-block. Note that this will wait forever if any given unit never terminates (by itself or by getting stopped explicitly); particularly services which use "RemainAfterExit=yes".
Talk to the service manager of the system. This is the implied default.
Do not send wall message before halt, power-off and reboot.
When used with enable and disable, operate on the global user configuration directory, thus enabling or disabling a unit file globally for all future logins of all users.
When used with enable, disable, preset, mask, or unmask, do not implicitly reload daemon configuration after executing the changes.

When used with kill, choose which processes to send a UNIX process signal to. Must be one of main, control, cgroup or all to select whether to kill only the main process, the control process, all processes in the unit's control group or all processes of the unit.

If used with the kill command, enqueues a signal along with the specified integer value parameter to the specified process(es). This operation is only available for POSIX Realtime Signals (i.e. --signal=SIGRTMIN+...

Takes a control group sub-path to send signals to, for use with the kill command. By default the chosen signal is delivered to all processes of the unit's cgroups (as well as the main/control processes (if outside) – subject to --kill-whom=). But with this option a subgroup can be selelected instead.
When used with kill, choose which signal to send to selected processes. Must be one of the well-known signal specifiers such as SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGSTOP. If omitted, defaults to SIGTERM.

Select what type of per-unit resources to remove when the clean command is invoked, see above. Takes one of configuration, state, cache, logs, runtime, fdstore to select the type of resource. This option may be specified more than once, in which case all specified resource types are removed.
When used with halt, poweroff or reboot, set a short message explaining the reason for the operation. The message will be logged together with the default shutdown message. Added in version 225.

When used with enable/disable/is-enabled (and related commands), use the specified root path when looking for unit files. If this option is present, systemctl will operate on the file system directly, instead of communicating with the systemd daemon to carry out changes.

Takes a path to a disk image file or block device node. If specified, all operations are applied to file system in the indicated disk image. This option is similar to --root=, but operates on file systems stored in disk images or block devices.

Takes an image policy string as argument, as per systemd.image-policy(7). The policy is enforced when operating on the disk image specified via --image=, see above. If not specified, defaults to the "*" policy, i.e. all recognized file systems in the image are used.

Takes one of "full" (the default), "enable-only", "disable-only". When used with the preset or preset-all commands, controls whether units shall be disabled and enabled according to the preset rules, or only enabled, or only disabled. Added in version 215.
When used with status, controls the number of journal lines to show, counting from the most recent ones. Takes a positive integer argument, or 0 to disable journal output. Defaults to 10.
When used with status, controls the formatting of the journal entries that are shown. For the available choices, see journalctl(1). Defaults to "short".

When used with the reboot, poweroff, or halt command, indicate to the system's firmware to reboot into the firmware setup interface for the next boot. Note that this functionality is not available on all systems. Added in version 220.

When used with the reboot, poweroff, or halt command, indicate to the system's boot loader to show the boot loader menu on the following boot. Takes a time value as parameter —— indicating the menu timeout. Pass zero in order to disable the menu timeout. Note that not all boot loaders support this functionality.

When used with the reboot, poweroff, or halt command, indicate to the system's boot loader to boot into a specific boot loader entry on the following boot. Takes a boot loader entry identifier as argument, or "help" in order to list available entries. Note that not all boot loaders support this functionality.

This switch is used with reboot. The value is architecture and firmware specific. As an example, "recovery" might be used to trigger system recovery, and "fota" might be used to trigger a “firmware over the air” update. Added in version 246.
When used with list-dependencies, list-units or list-machines, the output is printed as a list instead of a tree, and the bullet circles are omitted. Added in version 203.

Change the format of printed timestamps. The following values may be used: pretty (this is the default) "Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS TZ" Added in version 248. unix "@seconds-since-the-epoch" Added in version 251. us, μs "Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.UUUUUU TZ" Added in version 248. utc "Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC" Added in version 248.

When used with bind, creates the destination file or directory before applying the bind mount. Note that even though the name of this option suggests that it is suitable only for directories, this option also creates the destination file node to mount over if the object to mount is not a directory, but a regular file, device…
When used with bind, creates a read-only bind mount. Added in version 248.
When used with edit, use NAME as the drop-in file name instead of override.conf. Added in version 253.

When used with halt, poweroff, reboot or kexec, schedule the action to be performed at the given timestamp, which should adhere to the syntax documented in systemd.time(7) section "PARSING TIMESTAMPS".
When used with edit, the contents of the file will be read from standard input and the editor will not be launched. In this mode, the old contents of the file are completely replaced.

Execute the operation remotely. Specify a hostname, or a username and hostname separated by "@", to connect to. The hostname may optionally be suffixed by a port ssh is listening on, separated by ":", and then a container name, separated by "/", which connects directly to a specific container on the specified host.
Execute operation on a local container. Specify a container name to connect to, optionally prefixed by a user name to connect as and a separating "@" character.
Execute operation on a capsule. Specify a capsule name to connect to. See capsule@.service(5) for details about capsules. Added in version 256.
Do not query the user for authentication for privileged operations.
Enable or disable printing of the legend, i.e. column headers and the footer with hints. The legend is printed by default, unless disabled with --quiet or similar.
Print a short help text and exit.
Print a short version string and exit.
